reading.body:
The five most-starred open-source multi-agent frameworks have accumulated nearly 184,000 combined GitHub stars, with the two leaders, autogen and crewAI, each exceeding 57,000, signaling that agent orchestration has become one of the most actively tracked problems in applied AI.

The pattern across these repositories is convergence on Python as the implementation language and permissive licensing, with Apache-2.0 and MIT each covering two projects and CC-BY-4.0 covering one. All five remain unarchived and were pushed within the last year of the generation date, indicating active maintenance rather than abandoned experiments. The A2A repository stands apart in purpose: where the others provide frameworks for building agents, A2A defines a protocol for communication between agents built in different frameworks, suggesting the field is moving toward interoperability as a distinct engineering concern.

For AI infrastructure, the significance is indirect but real. Multi-agent systems multiply the number of model calls required to complete a task, since each agent invocation draws on compute and each coordination step adds latency and token consumption. Wider adoption of these frameworks therefore translates into higher sustained inference load, which feeds back into demand for power and data-center capacity. The data does not speak to deployment scale, actual usage, or the compute intensity of any specific workload, so the connection to grid pressure is directional rather than quantified.

What the data does not cover is equally important to note. Star counts measure developer interest, not production adoption. The repositories vary in maturity and stated purpose, with OpenAI's swarm explicitly labeled educational. No information is given on the number of active contributors, downstream dependents, or commercial deployments, so no claim about market share or real-world impact can be drawn from these figures alone.
